summary: Year 3 learners (age 7-8) compare and order unit fractions (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5) and same-denominator fractions (1/5...4/5). Two directions that feel contradictory must be held together: for unit fractions a LARGER denominator means a SMALLER fraction (the whole is cut into more, smaller pieces), while for same-denominator fractions a LARGER numerator means a LARGER fraction (more of the same-sized piece). These are not one rule reversing; they compare different varying quantities. Ground both in piece size using aligned bars and a shared number line so children do not over-generalise a blanket 'bigger bottom = smaller'.
misconceptions: Whole-number bias — orders unit fractions 1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2 (bigger denominator judged bigger)
Over-correction — after learning 'bigger bottom = smaller', reverses same-denominator fractions too (1/5 > 2/5 > 3/5)
Compares numerators and denominators independently rather than as one quantity
Cannot place the fractions consistently on a number line to check the order
Ignores that the whole must be the same when comparing

activities.title: Order unit fractions under one shared whole
steps: Take fraction cards 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 and arrange them from largest to smallest.

Represent each card as a bar the same length as a single common '1 whole' bar, split into that many equal parts with one part shaded, and line the bars up beneath that '1 whole' so the shaded pieces can be compared by length.
State and check the order: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest, confirming 1/5 is the shortest and 1/2 the longest.
Explain out loud why 1/2 is bigger than 1/5 by pointing at the piece lengths against the same whole.
activities.insight: When the whole is the same, a unit fraction with a larger denominator is smaller because the whole is split into more, smaller pieces.

activities.title: Cut into more pieces and feel each one shrink
steps: Start with one whole and partition it into 2, then 3, then 4, then 5 equal pieces, each time comparing the size of a single piece to the previous one.
Describe what happens to the size of each piece as more cuts are added.
Connect the action back to the cards: more pieces (bigger denominator) means each piece, and so each unit fraction, is smaller.
activities.insight: Cutting a fixed whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller, so more pieces means a smaller unit fraction.

activities.title: Order same-denominator fractions by counting the same-sized piece
steps: Take fifths fractions 1/5, 2/5, 3/5, 4/5 and order them from largest to smallest, keeping the piece size (one fifth) fixed.
Represent each as a bar where only the number of shaded fifths changes, and check that 4/5 covers more of the bar than 2/5.
State the order 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5 and explain that more fifths means more because each piece is the same size.
activities.insight: When the denominator is fixed, the numerator counts how many of the same-sized piece, so a larger numerator means a larger fraction.

activities.title: Place and read the fractions on a shared number line
steps: Place each fraction from both sets onto one shared number line between 0 and 1, consistent with its order.
Decide where 3/5 sits compared with 1/2 and judge whether it is bigger or smaller.
Use position on the line to check that the unit-fraction order and the fifths order agree with where each fraction lands.

Try a mixed set (e.g. 1/5, 1/2, 3/5) and use positions on the number line, together with the two rules, to order it; note that neither rule on its own can compare fractions such as 3/5 and 1/2, where both the numerator and the denominator differ.
activities.insight: Both comparisons can be read as position on one number line, which unifies the unit-fraction and same-denominator cases into a single idea of magnitude.

activities.title: Practise and check the orderings
steps: Order 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest as an ordering task.

Compare 2/5 and 4/5 and choose the larger, explaining the choice; be alert to the tempting wrong answer of picking 2/5 by over-applying 'bigger bottom = smaller' to a comparison where only the numerator differs.
Place a given fraction at the right spot on a number line as a final check.
activities.insight: Fluent, correct ordering of both fraction types, with the reasoning articulated, confirms the magnitude idea has taken hold.

checkQuestion: Here are four fraction cards: 1/2, 1/5, 1/3, 1/4. Put them in order from LARGEST to smallest. Now here are four more: 3/5, 1/5, 4/5, 2/5 — put these in order from largest to smallest too. As you go, place each fraction on this number line. [Watch how the child orders each set and where they place the cards.]
checkAnswer: Unit fractions largest→smallest: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 (larger denominator = smaller piece). Same-denominator fractions largest→smallest: 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5 (more fifths = more). Each card placed consistently on the number line matching its order.
